Ancient Egypt was predominantly patriarchal. It was not a matriarchy. Men normally held the highest political, administrative, and military positions. Women could possess considerable rights and sometimes rule, but the general structure privileged male authority. That is what the surviving evidence supports. 
Did women have power over men? Yes—some women unquestionably did. That is different from women generally being the ruling sex.
- A female pharaoh had authority over male subjects and officials. Hatshepsut exercised the full powers of kingship as senior co-ruler with Thutmose III. Her authority was governmental, not merely influence over a husband. 
- Some religious officeholders headed major institutions employing men. The God’s Wife of Amun controlled a substantial estate with male administrators. For example, Harwa served as high steward under Amenirdis I. 
- Women could exercise enforceable rights against men. They could own property, make contracts, and bring cases to court independently. A man’s sex did not automatically give him ownership of a woman’s possessions or immunity from her legal claims. 
Why, then, call it patriarchal? Because those possibilities existed within a society where leadership was overwhelmingly male and women’s expected social position centred on marriage, motherhood, and household management. Men were commonly identified by their offices and occupations; women were often identified through their husbands or fathers. 
We also have explicit statements of male authority. The Instructions of Ptahhotep, in the translation discussed by Egyptologist Janet Johnson, advises a husband concerning his wife: “Keep her from power, restrain her.” That is evidence of a prescriptive male-dominant ideal. It does not establish that every husband successfully controlled his wife, or that women lacked legal independence. 
A female monarch’s existence does not establish a matriarchy: her position shows that royal rank could put a woman above men within an otherwise male-dominated hierarchy. Similarly, women owning property establishes economic rights, not female supremacy.

The Rule of 72: How To Double Your Money (Einstein’s Secret)

Do you know exactly how many years it takes to double your money? You don’t need a financial advisor to figure it out. There is a simple math rule that Albert Einstein himself called a genius concept.

This is the Rule of 72. Just divide 72 by your annual return rate, and you get the exact number of years it will take for your money to double. If your money is in an FD earning 6%, it will take 12 years to double. But if it’s in an index fund earning 12%, it will take just 6 years. The difference between 6% and 12% is not just a number—it’s the difference between 3x growth and 8x growth over 20 years. 

Compounding is the eighth wonder of the world. Those who understand it earn it; those who don’t, pay for it.

Why A ₹1 Lakh Salary Keeps You Poor (The Income Illusion)

A man worked for 40 years and earned ₹1 lakh per month. Yet, he retired with zero savings. Where did the money go?

This is the Income Illusion. We think a higher salary automatically makes us rich. But if you earn ₹1 lakh and spend ₹95,000, you are broke. Thomas Stanley proved this in “The Millionaire Next Door”—high income doesn’t equal high wealth. Every salary hike gets eaten by a new EMI and lifestyle upgrades. 

The real rich don’t just earn a high salary. They build assets that generate cash flow without them having to work. Your salary makes you a living, your assets make you wealthy.
